title: Encoding/Decoding (orig. 'Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse', CCCS Stencilled Paper 7, 1973; repr. in Culture, Media, Language 1980)
key_findings: Encoding and decoding are distinct 'determinate moments'; there is 'no necessary correspondence' between the meaning encoded and the meaning decoded.
Visual codes look 'natural' only through habituation; naturalized codes are learned and culture-specific.
Connotative domains are organised into 'preferred readings' that carry the dominant social order, but polysemy is not pluralism.
Three hypothetical decoding positions: dominant-hegemonic, negotiated (accepts the general frame, adapts to 'local conditions'), oppositional.
practical_applications: Before publishing, ask how each audience segment could decode the piece: preferred, negotiated, oppositional.
Treat 'obvious' visual signs (gestures, colours, uniforms) as learned codes that need testing with outsiders.
limitations: Theoretical essay about broadcast TV, not an empirical audience study; later reception research (Morley) tested and complicated it.

title: Stuart Hall (University of Birmingham 'Perspective' article on Hall and the CCCS)
key_findings: Hall joined Richard Hoggart's new Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) in 1964 as Research Fellow, left in 1979 for the Open University.
The Centre studied everyday popular culture: youth cultures, the press, film and television; collaborative books include Resistance Through Rituals, Policing the Crisis and Culture, Media, Language.
Hall treated cultural studies as 'a field of enquiry' rather than a discipline; best-known for encoding/decoding and for how age, class, race and gender interact with dominant ways of seeing.
The University closed the Department of Cultural Studies and Sociology in 2002.
practical_applications: Use CCCS framing: popular and everyday culture (memes, BL fandom, festival content) is worth serious analysis.
limitations: University commemorative article (no explicit year; 50th-anniversary context suggests 2014); not a critical history.

title: Conditions of their Own Making: An Intellectual History of the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies at the University of Birmingham
key_findings: Intellectual history of the CCCS: historical context, organisational difficulties, activist aspirations and tensions participants felt between intellectual and political objectives.
practical_applications: Reminder that cultural studies is explicitly political (power, class, race), unlike value-dimension models.
limitations: Only the abstract was read.

title: Raymond Williams: 'Culture is Ordinary' (review article)
doi_isbn: ARIEL: A Review of International English Literature
key_findings: 'Culture is ordinary' was the key theme of Williams's career: culture is not for the discerning few but for the many, and joins people in community.
Williams wrote as a voice of the working class and of Wales; his work stressed the collective nature of ideas, language and values.
practical_applications: Design for 'ordinary culture' (daily routines, family, food, local speech) rather than only high-culture or postcard symbols.
limitations: Read only the opening/abstract text; Williams's own 1958 essay was not read this session.

title: Notes in the history of intercultural communication: The Foreign Service Institute and the mandate for intercultural training
key_findings: E. T. Hall's The Silent Language (1959) is generally listed as the first work of intercultural communication.
Hall's work rested on training American diplomats at the Foreign Service Institute, 1946-1956, with linguists and anthropologists.
practical_applications: Intercultural communication began as applied training for practitioners; its country typologies were built for briefing, not prediction.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Quantitative Research in Proxemic Behavior
authors: Watson, O. Michael; Graves, Theodore D.
key_findings: Hall coined 'proxemics' and devised a notation; his Arab vs American observations were impressionistic.
Controlled observation of 32 Arab and American students: Arabs interacted closer and more directly than Americans, as hypothesised.
practical_applications: Distance and orientation between characters are culturally read; stage them deliberately.
limitations: Tiny student sample, two groups only; abstract only.

title: Preferred interpersonal distances: A global comparison
authors: Sorokowska, A.; Sorokowski, P.; Hilpert, P.; Cantarero, K.; Frackowiak, T. et al.
key_findings: N = 8,943 participants from 42 countries; preferred social, personal and intimate distances measured.
Age and gender influence space preferences; some variation is explained by regional temperature.
practical_applications: Use as reference values for blocking characters (stranger vs acquaintance vs close person).
limitations: Self-report on a graphic scale, not observed behaviour; abstract read this session (an M17 registry note says Thailand was not sampled).

title: The Pace of Life in 31 Countries
key_findings: Pace of life measured by walking speed downtown, postal work speed and clock accuracy in large cities of 31 countries.
Fastest in Japan and Western Europe, slowest in economically undeveloped countries; faster in colder, economically productive and individualistic cultures.
practical_applications: Chronemics is measurable: timing norms (punctuality, speed) differ, so 'fast-cut urgency' is not neutral.
limitations: Big-city samples only; 1990s data; abstract only; Thailand's inclusion not verified.

title: The weirdest people in the world?
authors: Henrich, Joseph; Heine, Steven J.; Norenzayan, Ara
key_findings: Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33(2-3):61-83. A survey of top journals in six psychology sub-disciplines (2003-2007, via Arnett 2008) found 68% of subjects from the US and 96% from Western industrialized countries with 12% of the world's population.

WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) subjects are frequent outliers in domains including visual perception (Mueller-Lyer), fairness (Ultimatum/Dictator games), spatial reasoning, moral reasoning and self-concepts.
Researchers often generalise from undergraduates to the species without testing.
practical_applications: Treat Western-sample findings (ad psychology, colour, humour) as hypotheses for Thai audiences until tested locally.
limitations: Read the pre-publication UBC version (page numbers differ); argues variability, not that nothing generalises.

title: The neglected 95%: Why American psychology needs to become less American
key_findings: Analysis of six premier APA journals: contributors, samples and editors predominantly American, while Americans are under 5% of the world population.
practical_applications: Check where the samples behind a 'proven' persuasion tactic came from.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: The neglected 95% revisited: Is American psychology becoming less American?
authors: Thalmayer, Amber Gayle; Toscanelli, Cecilia; Arnett, Jeffrey Jensen
key_findings: Same six journals 2014-2018: authors and samples now a little over 60% American; increase mostly from other English-speaking and Western European countries.
About 11% of the world population is represented; majority-world authors and samples only 4-5%.
practical_applications: The WEIRD gap persists a decade later; Thai and SE Asian evidence remains scarce.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Beyond Western, Educated, Industrial, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) Psychology: Measuring and Mapping Scales of Cultural and Psychological Distance
authors: Muthukrishna, M.; Bell, A. V.; Henrich, J.; Curtin, C. M.; Gedranovich, A. et al.
key_findings: Applies the fixation index (FST) to World Values Survey data to measure cultural distance between any two countries, from the US and from China.
Cultural distance predicts various psychological outcomes; the US is relatively homogeneous regionally.
practical_applications: Use cultural distance (not a WEIRD/non-WEIRD binary) to judge how far a foreign finding may transfer to Thailand.
limitations: Abstract only; Thailand's specific distance not read.

title: An Overview of the Schwartz Theory of Basic Values
key_findings: Ten basic personal values recognised across cultures, arranged in a circular motivational structure that is apparently culturally universal.
Measured with the Schwartz Value Survey and Portrait Values Questionnaire; evidence from 82 countries.
Substantial individual differences in value priorities, yet the average value hierarchy of most societal groups is similar.
practical_applications: Brief characters and audiences on individual values (e.g. benevolence vs achievement) rather than nationality.
limitations: Abstract only (full text blocked, HTTP 403).

title: A Theory of Cultural Value Orientations: Explication and Applications
key_findings: Seven cultural value orientations forming three dimensions, derived a priori; validated with data from 73 countries.
Mapping of 76 national cultures into 7 transnational groupings (West European, English-speaking, Latin American, East European, South Asian, Confucian-influenced, African and Middle Eastern).
practical_applications: A theory-driven alternative to Hofstede for country-level briefs.
limitations: Abstract only; Thailand's grouping not verified this session.

title: National Culture and the Values of Organizational Employees: A Dimensional Analysis Across 43 Nations
authors: Smith, Peter B.; Dugan, Shaun; Trompenaars, Fons
key_findings: 8,841 managers/employees in 43 countries; items on universalism-particularism, achievement-ascription, individualism-collectivism.

Multidimensional scaling found three interpretable dimensions, largely consistent with earlier surveys; Hofstede's IDV and PDI may be better defined as loyal vs utilitarian involvement and conservatism vs egalitarian commitment.
practical_applications: Trompenaars' own data reduce to fewer dimensions than his seven-dimension business model.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Riding the waves of commerce: A test of Trompenaars' 'model' of national culture differences
key_findings: Re-analysis of Trompenaars' database: the seven-dimension theory in the book is not supported by the data; the dimensions found correlate with Hofstede's Individualism (per search summary of the abstract).
practical_applications: Popular consultancy models (Trompenaars' seven dimensions) are weaker than their training slides suggest.
limitations: Only a search summary of the abstract; Trompenaars & Hampden-Turner replied (not read).

title: Is National Culture a Meaningful Concept? Cultural Values Delineate Homogeneous National Clusters of In-Country Regions
key_findings: World Values Survey data: 299 in-country regions from 28 countries (East and Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, Anglo world) overwhelmingly cluster along national lines on basic values.
Holds even for Malaysia vs Indonesia despite shared language, religion and ethnic groups.
practical_applications: Counterpoint to the critics: national means are not meaningless; they describe groups, not individuals.
limitations: Abstract only; regional clustering of means does not remove large within-country individual variance (Taras 2016).

title: The Ecological Fallacy in National Culture Research
key_findings: Hofstede and GLOBE scales correlated at the national (ecological) level are not correlated the same way at individual or organisational level; projecting them down is an ecological fallacy.
Five articles in top journals commit this fallacy; consequences include invalid theory and 'persistence of erroneous practitioner stereotyping'.
practical_applications: Never write 'Thai customers are collectivist, so this customer...' in a brief.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Does Country Equate with Culture? Beyond Geography in the Search for Cultural Boundaries
authors: Taras, Vas; Steel, Piers; Kirkman, Bradley L.
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 558 studies using Hofstede's framework: approximately 80% of variation in cultural values resides within countries; 'country is often a poor proxy for culture'.

Occupation, socioeconomic status, wealth, political freedom, globalisation and instability were tested; per press coverage, occupation and SES outperformed country on power distance and individualism but not on uncertainty avoidance.
practical_applications: Segment by occupation, class, age or lifestyle before nationality.
limitations: Abstract (via RePEc) plus press summaries; per-dimension percentages not verified in the paper.

title: Dimensions and Dynamics of National Culture: Synthesizing Hofstede With Inglehart
key_findings: EVS/WVS data on 495,011 individuals born 1900-1999 in 110 countries: younger generations have become more individualistic and more joyous.
Economic development and generational replacement drive change, yet roughly half of the variation in national cultural orientations is unique to each country.
practical_applications: Thai Gen Z is not Komin's 1970s sample; check generation before using 'Thai values'.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Country comparison tool: Thailand (Hofstede 6-D scores and text)
authors: The Culture Factor Group (formerly Hofstede Insights)
key_findings: Thailand: Power Distance 64, Individualism 19, Motivation towards Achievement (formerly Masculinity) 34, Uncertainty Avoidance 64, Long Term Orientation 67, Indulgence 45 (page read 2026-11-26).
Text calls Thailand highly collectivist, the lowest-scoring in Asia on MAS (Asian average 53), and links scores to kreng jai, mai pen rai and sanuk.
practical_applications: Starting hypotheses for a market brief only.
limitations: Commercial consultancy page; older secondary sources list different values (e.g. IDV 20 and other LTO values), so scores have been revised; descriptive text stereotypes.

title: Cultural Value Adaptation in Advertising is Effective, But Not Dependable: A Meta-Analysis of 25 Years of Experimental Research
authors: Hornikx, Jos; Janssen, Anne; O'Keefe, Daniel J.
key_findings: About 120 comparisons of adapted vs unadapted value appeals: effects exist but are small (persuasion mean r = .049; ad liking mean r = .055).
Adaptation effects have diminished over time (year vs persuasion r = -.152; vs liking r = -.185).
The effects do not allow dependable advice for practitioners.
practical_applications: Value-matching is a weak lever; avoiding offence and testing with insiders matter more.
limitations: Abstract read this session (International Journal of Business Communication).

title: A Meta-Analysis of Studies on the Determinants of Standardization and Localization of International Marketing and Advertising Strategies
authors: Cheon, Hongsik John; Cho, Chang-Hoan; Sutherland, John
key_findings: 1,268 statistical models in 152 studies (1960-2004, 10 journals): support for standardisation of marketing mix and organisation factors.
Advertising moderators - affective appeals, executions, and receiver attitudes/values/customs - are strongly influenced by localisation.
practical_applications: Standardise the brand system (logo, product truth, price logic); localise the emotional appeal and execution.
limitations: Abstract only; literature to 2004, pre-social-media.

title: Identifying Global and Culture-Specific Dimensions of Humor in Advertising: A Multinational Analysis
authors: Alden, Dana L.; Hoyer, Wayne D.; Lee, Chol
key_findings: Content analysis of humorous TV ads from Korea, Germany, Thailand and the US.
Humorous ads share universal cognitive structures (incongruity), but specific content varies along normative dimensions such as collectivism-individualism.
practical_applications: Keep the incongruity structure; localise who and what the joke is about.
limitations: Abstract only; 1990s TV ads.

title: Managing Images in Different Cultures: A Cross-National Study of Color Meanings and Preferences
authors: Madden, Thomas J.; Hewett, Kelly; Roth, Martin S.
key_findings: Eight-country study of colour preferences and meanings: cross-cultural patterns of both similarity and dissimilarity.
Some colour combinations for a logo show consistent meaning across countries, others complementary meanings.
practical_applications: Test brand colour meaning per audience instead of trusting colour-meaning charts.
limitations: Abstract only; which eight countries not verified; student samples typical.

title: Cultural Superstitions and the Price Endings Used in Chinese Advertising
authors: Simmons, Lee C.; Schindler, Robert M.
key_findings: 499 prices from newspaper ads (Jan-Feb 1996) in Shanghai, Hong Kong and Taiwan; ending-digit distribution differs strongly from chance (chi2(9) = 576.97).
8 was the most common rightmost salient ending digit (Shanghai 58.1%, Hong Kong 47%, Taiwan 24.8%); 4 was rare (0%, 2%, 1.5%).
Effect consistent across communities and price representations.
practical_applications: For Chinese visitors, avoid 4 in prices and promo numbers; 8 is a positive signal.
limitations: Describes advertiser behaviour in 1996, not consumer response; Chinese communities only.

title: Creating speech register in Thai conversation
key_findings: Thai speakers build register from formality particles, pronominals, names, kin terms, titles and pragmatic particles; varied frequencies and combinations create shades of register.
Strangers in unfamiliar situations negotiate a middle-ground register.
practical_applications: Pick pronouns, kin terms and particles per relationship in scripts and VO (khun/phi/nong, khrap/kha).
limitations: Four conversations analysed; abstract only.

title: Contesting Isan-ness: discourses of politics and identity in Northeast Thailand
key_findings: Isan ethnoregional identity is a problematic political construct, negotiated against Thai and Lao identities, with cultural, social and political ramifications.
practical_applications: Do not reduce Isan to a comic accent or maid role; identity is plural and contested.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: From Melayu Patani to Thai Muslim: The Spectre of Ethnic Identity in Southern Thailand
key_findings: Representations of people in the southern border provinces since WWII: competing discourses of Thai national, Malay ethnic, Muslim and local Patani identities.
practical_applications: Labels matter: 'Thai Muslim', 'Malay Muslim' and 'Patani' carry different politics; avoid conflict imagery as decoration.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: Flexible Identity: Unfolding the Identity of the Chinese-Thai Population in Contemporary Thailand
key_findings: Argues against Skinner's total-assimilation prediction: hybridity and cultural flexibility let Chinese descendants be Thai as well as Chinese.
Identity politics operate at village, national and transnational levels.
practical_applications: Chinese New Year content can address Chinese-Thai customers as insiders, not foreigners.
limitations: Undergraduate research journal (The Arbutus Review); abstract only.

title: Tolerance but not Inclusion: A national survey on experiences of discrimination and social attitudes towards LGBT people in Thailand
key_findings: Released 2 Dec 2019; survey of 2,210 people (1,349 LGBT, 861 non-LGBT) plus focus groups in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phitsanulok, Pattani.

Overall favourable attitudes towards LGBT people, but acceptance drops for LGBT family members, co-workers and students; most LGBT respondents reported at least one form of discrimination; only 44% knew the Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558.
practical_applications: Visibility is not inclusion: show LGBTQ+ people in ordinary family/work roles, not as comic relief.
limitations: Only press materials via search summary; UNDP pages returned HTTP 403.

title: Economic Inclusion of LGBTI Groups in Thailand
authors: World Bank Group (with Thammasat University, Love Frankie, Nordic Trust Fund)
key_findings: Thailand is widely considered progressive among developing countries on LGBTI inclusion, yet LGBTI people experience discrimination and barriers in jobs, housing and services.
First large quantitative survey of LGBTI economic outcomes in Thailand, with a representative non-LGBTI reference group and 19 life-story interviews.
practical_applications: Same lesson: the 'tolerant Thailand' image hides exclusion; avoid tokenism.
limitations: Online survey of LGBTI respondents (self-selected); abstract only.

title: Jubilation as Thailand's marriage equality law comes into effect
key_findings: Law took effect 23 January 2025; gender-neutral terms replace 'men/women/husbands/wives'; same adoption and inheritance rights, medical decision rights, spousal benefits.
Thailand is the first Southeast Asian country and third in Asia (after Taiwan and Nepal) to legalise same-sex marriage; much of the country remains traditional and conservative.
practical_applications: Wedding/couple content for eyewear or gifts can include same-sex couples as ordinary customers.
limitations: News report; Thai government PR site gave 22 Jan as effective date (search result).

title: Thai boys love series and idols: a new facet of soft power diplomacy in Thailand
key_findings: Between 2014 and 2024 at least 250 Thai BL dramas were broadcast, mainly via international streaming platforms; fan bases abroad reach as far as Brazil.
'Affective economics' business model: revenue from constant idol-fan interaction (fan meetings, live streams); 2025 BL revenue projected at USD 144 million (citing The Economist).
The MFA mobilised BL series and idols (with GMMTV) for soft power; promotion signals LGBT+ openness and helps legitimate governments.
practical_applications: Thai popular culture (BL, Y content) is a real export audience; foreign fans know Thai pop culture better than postcard Thailand.
limitations: Qualitative historical analysis; secondary numbers from press; author notes non-state actors are marginalised in the study.

title: Digital 2025: Thailand
key_findings: Published 3 Mar 2025, data early 2025: population 71.6M, median age 40.6, 54.7% urban; internet users 65.4M (91.2%).
Ad reach: Facebook 51.0M (71.1%), YouTube 47.6M, LINE 56M MAU (78.2%), Messenger 35.9M, TikTok 34.0M adults 18+, Instagram 18.5M (25.8%), X 13.4M.
practical_applications: Thai reach is Facebook + LINE + YouTube first; Instagram reaches about a quarter of the population.
limitations: Ad reach is not active users; platforms revise figures; do not compare across sources or years.

title: Digital 2026: Thailand
key_findings: Published 8 Nov 2025, data Oct/late 2025: internet users 67.8M (94.7%); social media user identities 56.6M (79.1%); median age 40.6; 55.2% urban.
Ad reach: Facebook 51.5M (71.9%), YouTube 47.2M (65.9%), TikTok 56.6M users 18+ (96.3% of adults), LINE 56M MAU, Messenger 36.5M, Instagram 20.6M (28.7%), X 13.3M.
practical_applications: Plan Thai distribution around FB, LINE, TikTok, YouTube; IG Reels is a smaller, younger/urban slice.
limitations: Ad audience estimates, not users; TikTok figure swings strongly between reports; caution with changes.

title: Songkran in Thailand, traditional Thai New Year festival (Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, 18.COM, decision 8.B.10)
key_findings: Inscribed 2023 (18.COM). Songkran is in mid-April, marking the sun's passage into Aries.
Practices: family reunion, paying respect to older adults, ancestors and sacred Buddha images, pouring water (cleansing, reverence, good fortune), bathing Buddha images, folk plays, games, feasting.
Promotes community cooperation, unity and forgiveness; emphasis on elders helps combat loneliness.
practical_applications: Songkran content: lead with family, elders and blessing (rod nam dam hua), not only water fights.
limitations: Official nomination-based description (state-curated, idealised); regional variants not described.

title: BMA collects 391,027 krathongs in 2025 Loy Krathong festival, continuing decline trend
key_findings: 6 Nov 2025: BMA collected 391,027 krathongs (-24% vs 2024): natural materials 82.76%, foam 7.23%, bread 10.01%.
2024: 514,590 (98.39% natural); 2023: 639,828 (96.74% natural); online virtual krathongs fell to 23,347 from 36,832.
practical_applications: Loy Krathong content can carry an eco message, but avoid claiming 'foam is gone' - the 2025 share rose.
limitations: Bangkok only; categories changed in 2025 (bread separated); no causal explanation.

title: Religious composition and projections: Thailand (Future of World Religions country page)
key_findings: Buddhists projected to be about 91% and Muslims about 7% of Thailand's population in 2070; Thailand projected to have the largest Buddhist population of 201 countries/territories.
2020 baseline from census and survey data, later years are projections.
practical_applications: Buddhism is the default daily frame for Thai audiences; Muslims are the largest minority.
limitations: Projections; page has an inconsistent notice about 2010/2050 figures; NSO census figures (about 93-95% Buddhist) were seen only in secondary search results.

title: ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language - Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines
key_findings: Published June 2023; governing principles and guidelines for plain language documents, applicable to most written languages, examples in English.
Principles start from identifying readers and their purpose; annex with a sample checklist; mainly-text documents (videos outside scope).
practical_applications: English copy for international visitors: identify readers and purpose first; short, findable, usable text.
limitations: Paywalled; ISO page returned 403; only search summaries read.

title: Dolce & Gabbana Ad (With Chopsticks) Provokes Public Outrage in China
key_findings: Mid-Nov 2018: three Weibo videos showed an Asian model eating pizza, spaghetti and cannoli with chopsticks while a male voice in deliberately mispronounced Mandarin explained how to 'properly' eat.

Viewers called it racism and an outdated view of China; videos removed within 24 h; after alleged insulting messages by Stefano Gabbana went viral, performers withdrew and the 21 Nov Shanghai show was cancelled; Alibaba, JD.com and Lane Crawford pulled products; apology video 23 Nov.
practical_applications: A foreign brand 'teaching' locals their own culture as a joke = condescension; and context (founder behaviour) amplifies.
limitations: News report; long-term sales impact unclear.

title: Dunkin' Donuts apologises for 'racist' Thai ad
key_findings: 31 Aug 2013: Thai franchise's 'Charcoal Donut' campaign showed a smiling woman in blackface; Human Rights Watch called it 'bizarre and racist'.
Thai CEO Nadim Salhani called criticism 'paranoid American thinking'; US headquarters apologised and pulled the ad.
practical_applications: Local acceptance is no defence once content travels; global audiences decode with their own codes (Hall).
limitations: News report; Thai audience reaction only reported anecdotally (other outlets said the ad did not ruffle many in Thailand).

title: Unsung Hero (Thai Life Insurance, Ogilvy & Mather Bangkok) - Cannes Lions 'The Work' entry
key_findings: Per search summary of the entry: 2014 Cannes Lions shortlist; four weeks after launch 300,343,251 impressions, over 18 million engagements, 17 million video views.
Secondary commentary: soft-sell story about everyday kindness; brand appears only at the end.
practical_applications: Thai 'sad ad' storytelling (kindness, sacrifice, family) travels internationally when the story needs no Thai-language decoding.
limitations: Page body did not load; numbers are the entrant's claims via search snippet.

title: Thailand older persons statistics (NSO Survey of Older Persons; Department of Older Persons situation reports) - search summary
authors: National Statistical Office of Thailand; Department of Older Persons
key_findings: Secondary summaries: Thailand crossed the 'complete-aged society' threshold (60+ over 20% of population) around 2023-2024; NSO reported 13.64M aged 60+ (19.5%) in 2023; other sources give 20-21.6% for 2024.
practical_applications: Older Thais are a large audience: show them as active, capable customers, not as frail jokes.
limitations: Search snippets only; percentages differ by source and method.
